Bernoulli differential equation

We now consider a rather special type of equation that can be reduced to a linear equation by an
appropriate transformation. This is the so-called Bernoulli equation.
DEFINITION 1.
An equation of the form
                                      y ′ + p(x)y = q(x)y n                                      (1)

is called a Bernoulli differential equation.
We observe that if n = 0 or n = 1, then the Bernoulli equation (1) is actually a linear equation and is
therefore readily solvable as such. However, in the general case in which n ̸= 0 or n ̸= 1, this simple
situation does not hold and we must proceed in a different manner. We now state and prove theorem,
which gives a method of solution in the general case.
THEOREM.
Suppose n ̸= 0 and n ̸= 1. Then the transformation v = y 1−n reduces the Bernoulli equation (1) to a
linear equation in v.





Alexander Gladkov, Professor  (Belarusian State University)                 DIFFERENTIAL EQUATIONS                                  September 10, 2026                 3 / 54

Proof. We first multiply Equation (1) by y −n, thereby expressing it in the equivalent form

                                   y −ny ′ + p(x)y 1−n = q(x).                                   (2)

If we let v = y 1−n, then
                                    dv          −n dy                        = (1 −n)y
                                    dx             dx
and equation (2) transforms into
                                   1  dv
                          + p(x)v = q(x)
                                 1 −n dx
or, equivalently,
                              dv
                     + (1 −n)p(x)v = (1 −n)q(x).
                              dx





Alexander Gladkov, Professor  (Belarusian State University)                 DIFFERENTIAL EQUATIONS                                  September 10, 2026                 4 / 54

Letting
                                       p1(x) = (1 −n)p(x)

and
                                       q1(x) = (1 −n)q(x)

this may be written
                                    dv
                        + p1(x)v = q1(x)
                                    dx
which is linear in v. Theorem is proved.
Note that if n < 0 then y ̸= 0 and n > 0 then y ≡0 is a particular solution of (1).

Ricatti’s Equation
DEFINITION 2. Differential equation

                                y ′(x) = q0(x) + q1(x)y + q2(x)y 2                               (9)

where q0, q1, and q2 are given functions, with q0, q2 ̸≡0 is called Ricatti’s equation.
If q0 or q2 vanish identically on I, then (9) is reduced either to a Bernoulli equation for n = 2 or to a
linear first order DE, both of them previously studied.
In general, the solution of (9) cannot be obtained by means of integrals or, by another words, (9) is not
solved in quadratures (its general solution is not expressed through one or more integrals). However,
when we know a particular solution yp of (9), we are able to compute the general solution of that
equation by reducing it to a linear first-order DE by means of the substitution

First order DE not resolved with respect to the derivative.

We considered some methods of integration of first-order DE resolved with respect to the derivative.
Now we consider first-order DE which resolved with respect to dependent or independent variables.
First-order DE which resolved with respect to y.

Let we have DE in the following form
                                         y = ϕ(x, y ′).                                       (13)

Let p(x) = y ′(x) is a new function of x alone. Now we rewrite (13) in the following form

                                          y = ϕ(x, p).                                       (14)





Alexander Gladkov, Professor  (Belarusian State University)                 DIFFERENTIAL EQUATIONS                                  September 10, 2026                28 / 54

Differentiating (14) with respect to x then yields

                                p(x) = ϕ′x(x, p) + ϕ′p(x, p)p′(x).

This differential equation is resolved with respect to the derivative p′.
If an explicit function p = p(x, C) is a general solution of (15), then by substituting this function in
(14) one find a general solution of (13) as an explicit function y = ϕ(x, p(x, C)).
If an inverse function x = x(p, C) is a general solution of (15), then this function together with (14)
give a general solution in the parametric form x = x(p, C), y = ϕ(x(p, C), p), where p is a parameter.
If an implicit expression ψ(x, p, C) = 0 is a general solution of (15), then we have a general solution of
(13) as an implicit parametric relation y = ϕ(x, p), ψ(x, p, C) = 0.
